title: Trade credit: insuring the risk of non-payment
excerpt: How a business in Moldova can prepare a non-payment assessment: invoices, payment terms, buyers, receivables and conditions of potential trade credit insurance.

seo.title: Trade credit insurance in Moldova: non-payment risk | ING Broker
seo.description: Prepare receivables records, buyer limits and delivery documents for a trade credit assessment. Understand conditions without assuming every invoice is guaranteed.
seo.keywords: trade credit insurance Moldova, buyer non payment risk, receivables insurance, deferred payment sales, buyer credit limit

author: ING Broker editorial team
content:
Trade credit arises when a business supplies goods or services and allows its customer to pay later. Non-payment risk must be assessed separately from damaged cargo or warehouse losses. For a company in Moldova, discussion of trade credit insurance begins with invoices, payment terms and sales concentration by customer.

This article is informational and helps prepare an assessment. It does not confirm an offer for every company, buyer or overdue balance. Product availability, accepted buyers and the compensation mechanism require individual checking. Insurance should not be presented as guaranteed collection of every invoice or a replacement for receivables management.

Trade credit, bank borrowing and goods in transit

Separate the relationship with your customer from a loan your business takes from a bank. Here, a receivable is the amount owed by the buyer for a delivery or service. The debtor is the party required to pay. These explanations help read the file without determining the legal position of a particular case.

A CARGO policy concerns transported goods under its own conditions. It does not demonstrate that an invoice will be paid on time. Similarly, warehouse property insurance does not automatically resolve customer non-payment after delivery. Identify the precise loss being considered before comparing differently named products.

Build a verifiable receivables record

Prepare invoices by buyer, due date and currency. Separate amounts still within terms from overdue amounts and explain balance calculations. An accounting total alone does not describe the risk of a customer portfolio. Preserve the connection between order, delivery, invoice and payments already recorded.

Use consistent definitions in every file supplied. Explain invoices that have been corrected, returned or offset. Do not describe a disputed receivable as unreservedly accepted by the buyer. Mark unknown matters rather than filling them with assumptions to produce an apparently tidy file.

Sales concentration may matter more than customer numbers

Show how much deferred-payment sales depend on each important buyer. A business may have many customers while much of its outstanding balance comes from one. Initially, describe this dependency and periods when exposure increases without invented percentages or estimates presented as audited results.

Separate domestic sales from exports and new customers from those with a payment history. Identify relationships between companies where relevant. An established buyer or affiliated company is not automatically acceptable. Ask for the proposal's criteria and information needed to assess each debtor category.

What commercial documents establish

A contract, an order and a delivery record answer different questions. Identify the goods or service, buyer, agreed deadline and handover confirmation. For services, records of the delivered result and its acceptance may matter. The exact documents are agreed for the actual assessment, not established by a generic form.

If payment terms changed through correspondence or an amendment, preserve the applicable version. Do not assume every commercial change leaves possible insurance conditions unchanged. Ask about procedures for deadlines, limits and notification of changes before making decisions based on expected protection.

An overdue invoice does not establish the reason for non-payment

Distinguish administrative delay, lack of liquidity and a dispute over quality or quantity. A buyer disputing an invoice is not necessarily in the same position as one acknowledging the balance but unable to pay. Explaining the cause assists assessment but does not confirm an insured event.

Request definitions of accepted events, relevant periods and exclusions. Insolvency, prolonged default and other circumstances must be read in the proposed documents and legally reviewed where necessary. Do not automatically apply definitions or procedures from foreign contracts to a receivable arising in Moldova.

Buyer limits and actual exposure

If the proposal uses buyer limits, ask how they work and how they are confirmed. Show the existing balance, pending orders and planned deliveries. Exposure at a particular time is not always the same as annual sales to a customer. These differences should remain visible in the comparison.

Ask what happens when a balance exceeds a limit, the limit changes or payment becomes late. Continuing deliveries does not establish acceptance of every invoice. Request a written answer for the actual mechanism. A company's internal commercial limit is not automatically a limit approved by the insurer.

Which portion of the loss and which costs are assessed

Ask what part of a loss may remain with the business and which total limit applies. An excess or deductible is the part borne by the insured under the contract. Check recovery costs, interest and penalties rather than assuming they are included in an insured invoice amount.

For a hypothetical calculation, identify the eligible amount, partial payments, limit and assumptions. Do not present the example as an offer or promise for a real debtor. The insurer should explain its documents, while legal interpretation of the receivable requires a separate specialist assessment.

Compare prices against the portfolio and conditions

A premium is the amount paid for insurance. Ask for the calculation basis, period and reporting the proposal may require. A public rate or another firm's cost does not confirm your portfolio's price. Customer categories, terms and conditions should be described before comparing totals.

Also compare the internal administration time: who updates balances, monitors limits and sends notifications? These are organisational questions, not universal obligations established by this article. A proposal requiring reports the company cannot prepare accurately needs clarification before acceptance.

Track receipts and changes to payment terms

Maintain a clear procedure for partial payments, returns, corrections and offsets. Decide who monitors approaching due dates and contacts the buyer. Where a receivable is assessed within a policy, consult its instructions before extending terms, restructuring or taking other decisions that could affect the file.

Do not promise that an arrangement with the buyer will be accepted by the insurer without checking. Insurance does not remove the need for accurate commercial records. Keep debtor communications separate from insurer confirmations so the timeline can later be reconstructed without assumptions.

An example of checking an invoice internally

Imagine a deferred-payment delivery for which the buyer pays only part. Before assessment, allocate the payment to the correct invoice and determine the remaining balance. Record the date to which that reconciled balance applies. Check for returned goods, a price correction or disputed acceptance. Without reconciliation, the overdue amount in a file may not accurately describe the receivable.

The example is hypothetical and does not establish whether a particular loss qualifies under a contract. Ask how the balance is treated under the proposal, including later payments. Keep calculations and confirmations together so accounting, sales and the insurance contact work from the same verified position.

A preparation file for trade credit

  • Company activities and categories of goods or services sold.
  • Deferred-payment sales separated from advances and payment on delivery.
  • Major buyers, countries and relationships between companies.
  • Agreed terms and delivery confirmation procedures.
  • Balances, due dates and partial payments.
  • Disputed invoices, returns and contractual changes.
  • Experience of arrears and the internal monitoring procedure.
  • Requested exposure and questions about proposed limits.

Aggregated information and a contract sample without confidential data may be useful initially. Do not publish debtor lists, invoices or bank details in an open form. Buyer identities and detailed documents should be supplied only as needed for assessment, through the agreed channel. This file does not confirm portfolio eligibility.

When an invoice becomes overdue

Check recorded payments and the actual due date before drawing conclusions. Preserve delivery documents and the buyer's explanations. If a policy exists, consult its applicable notification procedure and request clarification. Do not copy a deadline or claims mechanism from another product's public page.

A policy purchased after the problem arises should not be presented as a guaranteed retrospective solution. Describe balances and known circumstances accurately. The broker can organise consideration of possibilities, but acceptance and claims decisions belong to the insurer under the contract. Legal debt recovery requires a separate assessment.

Frequently asked questions about trade credit insurance

Is this the same as insurance for a bank loan?

No. Here the risk concerns amounts owed by buyers for deferred-payment sales, under the conditions of an available product.

Can all late invoices be insured?

Do not assume an existing overdue amount will be accepted. Present the actual position, cause and timeline, then request an eligibility check.

Does CARGO guarantee payment for delivered goods?

Do not infer this. Protection of goods in transit and the buyer's non-payment risk are different subjects.

Does ING Broker guarantee collection of a receivable?

No. The company acts as a broker. Possible protection depends on product availability, risk acceptance and the insurer's conditions.
